Loud
loud
adj. (having great sound; noisy; rendering Hebrew gadol, Greek megas)
From Saxon hlud, loud. Scripture never treats volume as a virtue in itself: the same adjective marks the praise of heaven, the cry of the dying Saviour, and the woman whose loudness is the mark of her folly.

Biblical Definition

Loud describes volume, and Scripture judges it entirely by what is being said. In worship it is commanded and commended: “the Levites… stood up to praise the LORD God of Israel with a loud voice on high” (2 Chronicles 20:19), and the song of heaven itself is loud — “Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing” (Revelation 5:12). Loudness there is proportion, not excess; the worth of the Lamb warrants the volume. The most solemn loud voice in Scripture is our Lord's at the moment of death: “And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost” (Luke 23:46). A crucified man ordinarily died in exhaustion; the loud cry testifies that He laid down His life rather than merely lost it. But volume can equally mark folly, and Proverbs uses the adjective as a character diagnosis of the strange woman: “She is loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house” (Proverbs 7:11). Loudness there is joined to stubbornness and restlessness as one disposition.

Webster 1828 Definition

Having a great sound; noisy; striking the ear with force; clamorous. Scripture commends loud praise and records the loud cry of Christ at His death, while naming loudness joined to stubbornness as a mark of folly.

expand to see more

LOUD, a. [Sax. hlud; G. laut.] Having a great sound; noisy; striking the ear with great force; as, a loud voice; a loud cry.

2. Clamorous; noisy; as, a loud man; loud complaints.

3. Emphatical; impressive; as, a loud call for repentance.

LOUDLY, adv. With great sound or noise; noisily; also, clamorously; importunately.

LOUDNESS, n. Great sound or noise; as the loudness of a voice or of thunder.

2. Clamor; turbulence; uproar.

Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 20:19 — "And the Levites, of the children of the Kohathites, and of the children of the Korhites, stood up to praise the LORD God of Israel with a loud voice on high."

Revelation 5:12 — "Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing."

Luke 23:46 — "And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost."

Proverbs 7:11 — "(She is loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house:"

Modern Corruption

Volume has been mistaken for fervour, so that intensity of sound is read as intensity of devotion in worship and as strength of conviction in argument — neither of which Scripture grants.

expand to see more

Scripture commends loud praise and never equates loudness with sincerity. The Levites lifted their voices because of what they were saying, and the heavenly song is loud because the Lamb is worthy; in both cases the volume is answerable to the object. Where loudness becomes the instrument for producing feeling rather than the overflow of conviction about a Person, the order is inverted and worship begins to depend on the sound rather than on the truth. The test is simple enough to apply: remove the volume, and see whether anything is left that a congregation would still call worship.

The same confusion has moved into speech about doctrine, where volume and vehemence substitute for argument. Proverbs 7:11 is worth weighing here, since the loudness of the strange woman is listed as one symptom among a cluster — loud, stubborn, and never at home — which together sketch a character rather than a decibel level. Scripture's own model runs the other way: the still small voice at Horeb, a Servant who does not cry nor lift up his voice in the street, and a Saviour whose one recorded loud cry from the cross was a committal of His spirit into His Father's hands.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew idiom has no separate adjective for loud; it says qowl gadol, a great voice, and Greek follows with phone megale — the same construction rendered “loud voice” throughout the Authorized Version.

expand to see more

Hebrew qowl (H6963) — voice, sound, noise; the word joined to gadol to make a loud voice.

Hebrew gadol (H1419) — great, large; supplying the “loud” of a great voice in Hebrew idiom.

Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to murmur, roar, be clamorous; the verb behind the loud and stubborn woman of Proverbs 7:11.

Greek phone (G5456) — a voice, a sound; the noun in every “loud voice” of the New Testament.

Greek megas (G3173) — great; joined to phone for the loud cry of Luke 23:46 and Revelation 5:12.

Usage

"“Praise the LORD God of Israel with a loud voice on high” — volume answerable to its object is commended."

"“When Jesus had cried with a loud voice” — the strength of the cry testifies that He laid down His life."

"“She is loud and stubborn” — loudness joined to stubbornness sketches a character, not a volume."
